translations.title: From that pure and excellent gaze
translations.text:
From that pure and excellent gaze
come living spirits, all aflame;
received by my eyes, they pass
through me to where pain is felt.

They meet along the way with ease
my spirits, stirred by such a heat;
they leave me as though lost,
called by the good that stands before them.

Away, I picture her in memory;
my spirits, thinking they see her,
stir and kindle without measure.

But finding no easy path—
though hers, entering, melted theirs—
they burst to leave, with no way out.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: If I am wax to your will
translations.text:
If I am wax to your desire,
and your gaze alone my sun,
whose look inflames and conquers all
but those bereft of sense;

then comes a thing that, had I not
so often tried and seen it,
so contrary to reason's rule,
my own senses would not believe:

from far away your fiery gaze
sets me alight, so fiercely burning
I scarcely keep my life.

But if your eyes attack my wax,
I feel myself turn cold at once,
my blood congealing in its veins.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: If complaints and laments can do so much
translations.text:
If complaints and laments can do so much
as check the rivers' course,
and move the trees upon the shadowed hills
with their song;

if they made fierce tigers and cold rocks
stop to hear their weeping;
if, with less cause than mine,
they descended to the realms of dread,

why should my troubled life,
spent in misery and tears,
not soften a heart grown hard against me?

More pity should attend the voice
of one who weeps himself lost
than one who lost and weeps for something else.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Like the tender mother
translations.text:
As when a tender mother hears
her suffering child beg through tears
for something whose consumption
will double the pain he feels,

and loving pity will not let her
consider the harm she does;
she runs to give the thing he asks,
increasing pain, yet easing its attack,

so with my sick and foolish thought,
that asks you for its own undoing,
I would remove this deadly food.

But it asks, and every day it weeps
so much that I grant all it wants,
forgetting its death and even mine.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Let him who has lost so much lose no more
translations.text:
Let him who has lost so much lose no more;
love, let what I have suffered suffice.
Let my having once tried to defend myself
against your will now be my aid.

Your temple and its walls I dressed
with garments drenched by rain, adorned
as one who has escaped at last,
free from the storm he lived through.

I had sworn never again, by my own will,
to enter any danger like that one.
The oath was vain.

But I cannot save myself from what comes;
I do not break my promise here:
this danger is unlike the others, beyond my hand.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: By rugged roads I have arrived
translations.text:
By rugged roads I have arrived
at a place where fear can move me not;
if I try to change or take a step,
I am dragged back by the hair.

Yet with death beside me, I seek
new counsel for my life;
I know the best, yet choose the worst,
by habit's fault or fate's command.

On the other side, my brief span,
the errant course of all my years,
at their beginning and their middle;

my bent, with which I cease to fight,
the certain death that ends so many ills,
make me neglect my own repair.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: I feel the pain diminish little by little
translations.text:
I feel the pain grow less by little,
not because it has become more mild,
but feeling fails to feel it now,
so mad have I grown from feeling it.

I do not think I touch on madness
when I think of it; I glory in its sound,
and will not cease to seal it in and suffer,
though reason shrinks from doing so.

All harms me, sense and madness both:
one robs me of myself, because I am its own;
the other kills me, since I am its.

People will call it folly that I prize
the hurt in which I am destroyed;
I count it my one fortune.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Oh sweet tokens, found to my sorrow
translations.text:
Oh sweet tokens, found to my sorrow,
sweet and joyful when God so willed!
You dwell together in my memory,
conspiring there with my death.

Who would have told me, in those hours
when through you I saw such happiness,
that one day you would be shown to me
with pain so grave?

In a single hour you took away
the good you gave me bit by bit;
take me as well to meet the evil left.

Or I shall think you gave me all that joy
because you wished to see me die
among sad memories.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Suspicions, placed in my sad imagining
translations.text:
Suspicions, lodged in my sad imagining,
you war upon my senses, turning over
my afflicted breast with hard hands,
by night and day.

My resistance is at last exhausted,
the soul's strength spent; I yield,
repentant, letting you defeat me
for having struggled so long.

Lead me to that dreadful place
whose sight might show my death engraved;
until now I kept my eyes shut.

I lay my weapons down: the wretched
are granted no such lengthy defense.
Hang my spoils upon your chariot.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: My lady, if I endure apart from you
translations.text:
My lady, if I live apart from you
and do not die, it seems to me
I wrong the love I bear you,
and all the good I knew in your presence.

Then comes another turn of grief:
if I despair of life, I lose
all the good I hope for from you;
so what I feel is split in two.

My senses struggle in this division,
between your absence and their quarrel.
I no longer know what to do
within so vast a sorrow.

I never see them but at odds;
so fiercely they contend by night and day
that only in harming me do they agree.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: With utmost longing to see what lies
translations.text:
With desperate longing to see what lies
hidden in your heart's innermost place,
to learn if what is within agrees
in look and being with what shows outside,

I set my gaze upon it; but the hard
encounter with your beauty stops my eyes.
They cannot pass so far within
to see what your soul holds.

And so they stay, bereft, at the door
made by my pain, by that same hand
that spares not even your own breast;

there I saw my hope plainly dead,
and how Love's blow was struck in vain,
not passing beyond your gown.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: With such force and vigor joined
translations.text:
With such force and vigor joined,
the harsh winds conspire for my ruin;
they cut down my tender thoughts
as soon as they appeared above me.

The harm is that my cares survive
these onslaughts, safe from every blow;
they are hard and firmly rooted
through all my senses.

Yet on another side I do not grieve
that good has left me in its going,
for the grave pain within me lasts;

I clasp it close and take it for comfort,
for in a life so harshly journeyed
I shall cut short the road's own war.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: When I stop to contemplate my state
translations.text:
When I pause to contemplate my state
and see the steps that led me here,
I find that, though I lost my way,
I might have reached a worse disaster.

But once I forget that path,
I cannot tell how I came to such grief;
I know I am undone, and feel most keenly
my care dying along with me.

I shall be ended, having artlessly
surrendered to one who can destroy me
if she chooses—and know how to love it;

since my own will can kill me,
what will hers, so little on my side,
be able to do, if not just that?
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: At last I have come into your hands
translations.text:
At last I have come into your hands,
where I know I must die so pressed
that even easing care with complaints,
my only remedy, is forbidden me.

I do not know what has sustained my life,
unless I was kept alive so that in me alone
might be tested how keen a sword
can cut a man already conquered.

My tears were poured out where
hardness and drought gave them
bad fruit, as did my fate.

Let these tears I shed for you suffice.
Do not avenge yourself further on my weakness;
lady, take vengeance there with my death.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: I am forever bathed in tears
translations.text:
I am forever bathed in tears,
always breaking the air with sighs;
what hurts most is never daring to tell you
I have come to this state for you,

that seeing where I stand, how far I have gone
along the narrow road of following you,
if I turn back to flee from you,
I faint at what I left behind;

if I try to climb the difficult peak,
every step frightens me with examples
of those who fell along the way.

Above all, I lack the light of hope
that once let me travel through
the dark country of your oblivion.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: For a while my hope rises
translations.text:
For a while my hope rises.
So tired of having risen,
it falls again and, against my will,
leaves room for distrust.

Who could endure so harsh a change
from good to ill? O weary heart,
take courage in your misery:
a calm often follows fortune's storm.

With my own arms I shall undertake
to break a mountain none has broken,
thick with a thousand obstacles.

Death, prison, hindrance cannot keep me
from going to see you, whether I come
a naked spirit or in flesh and bone.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Within my soul was born of me
translations.text:
Within my soul there was conceived
by me a tender love; its birth
was welcomed by my feelings
as a longed-for only child.

But soon from it was born the one
who ruined all that loving thought,
trading its first delights away
for harshness and for torment.

Cruel grandson, giving life to your father
and killing your grandfather, why do you grow
so unlike the one from whom you came?

O jealous fear, whom do you resemble?
Envy, your own fierce mother,
shudders to see the monster she has borne.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Most illustrious Marquis
translations.text:
Most illustrious Marquis, upon whom
heaven pours all good the world can know,
if my pen could reach the lofty worth
that is the clear light of your flame,

and my voice proclaim your name,
high and profound, you alone would be
eternal, without equal—and through you
immortal would be the one who loves you.

All that the vast heavens desire,
all that the earth seeks after,
is found in you from side to side;

in you alone did nature form
an unheard-of image, never seen,
and art made equal to the thought.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Excelsior!
translations.text:
Why do miserable hearts,
why do lowly souls,
in life's fierce battles
neither struggle nor resist?

The human spirit grows more steadfast
the higher it ascends:
God placed the mud upon the plain,
and rock upon the mountain.

The white snow that melts so quickly
in deep and hollow valleys
remains upon the lofty peaks,
unchanging and eternal.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: To Voltaire
translations.text:
You are a mighty battering ram;
nothing withstands your satanic wit.
Even through the grave your strident
laughter rings again.

Your biting satire brought down
all that human folly held as true;
today reason alone guides
Adam's renewed descendants.

Now only the free religion of ideas
shapes their immortal destiny;
now miserable faith has fallen to earth;

Christ topples; torches light
up all the mysteries of the road.
You have won, Voltaire. Be damned!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: To Spain
translations.text:
Respect broken, obedience broken,
God's and law's restraints cast off,
you march through tears and mire,
storm winds beating at your face.

Seek no hidden cause, no unknown reason
for the evil eating at your heart:
your wickedness, like subtle poison,
drains the strength from your limbs.

Do not expect, in some convulsive revolt,
to find a cure by your own hand,
o rebellious and corrupted society!

You will pursue freedom in vain:
when a people forgets virtue,
its own vices bear its tyrant.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Sonnet
translations.text:
When blind and fallen spirits
pursue the light and hope in vain;
when their sovereign flight is struck down,
like a wounded condor in the sky;

when they seek refuge in forgetting,
only to be refused by its cold hand;
when ennui builds its barren nest
in the poor human heart;

when pain, stealing our calm,
offers our fierce longings nothing
but shadowed, desperate hours—

ah, immortality, dream of the soul
that yearns for the infinite! If you existed,
what barbarous torment you would be!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Photographs
translations.text:
Pantoja, take courage! Break the barrier:
shine on cards and letterheads;
beside the bull that hooked Pepete,
put yourself on sale in trinket shops.

You are a fool. “True—but hush your modesty;
let doubt not trouble you. What is one more fool
among the rabble, so full of childish pride,
wherever it turns up?”

You may be worth a peseta, good Pantoja!
Faces and names cast upon the world
by photography are worth little more.

Show us your face, and do not be amazed;
let the coming age gather up
so many portraits and so few men.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Introduction
translations.text:
These are times of struggle! Who can imagine
soft idleness in our restless age?
Amid the battle the poet sings,
the tribune speaks, the scholar writes.

No one feels the blow he gives or takes
as danger presses close: the strong athlete
falls defeated, and another readies himself
for the harsh fight.

The blind crowd rushes forward,
floods the field, advances in tumult,
with the sea's deep rumble.

In the fury stirring us, the voice is thunder
and lightning; art, a sword; science, a ram;
the idea, a storm.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Love!
translations.text:
O eternal Love, who in your deathless course
give life and motion to all beings,
with what ardent wonder do I feel you,
invisible, beating everywhere!

All creation is your slave,
it trembles and quickens with your breath;
your greatness is such that thought
would call you God, if God were not.

With your magnetic, fertile breath
you join the atoms none can touch;
you create, transform, illuminate,

and in the infinite sky, in the deep sea,
on the astonished earth, you reign—
Love, eternal Love, soul of the world!
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Twilight
translations.text:
The sun was touching its setting,
and the twilight's warm, uncertain light
wrapped all of nature round.

The two of us were alone,
silent with love and anxiousness,
hands clasped, trembling and burning,
watching the valley, sea, and quiet shore
slowly lose their color, clarity, and shape.

As night advanced in fearful hush,
our sadness deepened, harder to overcome.
At last, I know not how,
I, bewildered, you, wild,
our silent passion broke into a burning kiss.

Alas, when we returned with sighs
from that glorious ecstasy,
what did we see? A shadow in the sky,
and in our conscience, shadow.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: At the Stone Monastery (Aragon)
translations.text:
Let the atheist come and fix his gaze
on the swift cascades that fall
with thunder's crash, in the forest
that darkens day, filled with rustic harmony,
perfumes, and shadows;
on the titanic cave that awes him
with stone monsters, hidden lake,
and plunging river.
Faced with such grandeur, he will cry,
“Amazed, I believe in your sublime majesty, my God!”

Creation is a harp that sways
in tranquil vastness with eternal rhythm
and ringing song. No murmur, sound, or voice
in earth, sea, or wind fails to join
the immortal hymn's chorus.

The insect hidden in the grass,
the bird within its nest, thunder
in the cloud's entrails, even the flower
that blooms on graves—all send a note
in measured harmony ascending heavenward.

Never can man's blind arrogance,
though it drive him mad, attain
that august, sovereign power which bridles
the ocean and sets stars turning in the sky.

He may beat his brow in vain,
helpless in satanic, cursed pride;
like desperate Prometheus he will always
be pursued by desire—alas, as infinite as pain.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: To Quintana
translations.text:
To mark his coronation

There, in the flowering age
of my tranquil childhood,
when life's light hours slipped by in calm
and ardent ambition had not chased away
the soul's golden visions,
my good father would tell me,
in that tender, happy time,
the finest page in my homeland's history.

He told how one day, in endless mourning,
the proud eagle of Austerlitz and Jena
came from the banks of the Seine
to settle on our soil;
how the Castilian people, ablaze
with vibrant anger, fought against
genius and fortune. Hearing this strange tale,
I blessed God for setting my cradle
where glory's laurel grows.

“Innocent child,” I asked my father,
“who gave your sinewy arms their strength?
What mighty genius woke your brave spirit?
What sovereign, stirring voice kept energy
alive within your breasts?” My father wept
and answered: “The voice of great Quintana!
Spain trembled and groaned within that sound;
he voiced our nation's feeling,
the faithful echo of our glories.”

. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

From then I loved you; that affection
fled not like the soft illusions
that always charm a child's heart.
So now, upon your brow, the deathless laurel
shines, deep genius; it seems to me
I see crowned the giant effort
with which the Spanish people amazed the world.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Vertigo
translations.text:
Guarding the uncertain, narrow mouth
of an inlet, on a coastal crag
beaten by the sea day and night,
a giant, shadowed, ancient tower rises,
built by a king like a watch post
to defend the shore from sea's perils.

When storm winds do not shake its battlements,
not even the faintest murmur disturbs
the colossus' majesty. It rests
for long hours in profound stillness;
only the sound of some white gull,
nesting on the rock, beating the air,
can be heard.

But when the roaring sea strikes hard
against the steep rock that bars its way,
when the violent hurricane rages
along the towering wall, the castle,
steadfast in its place, defies
the wild symphony of wave and wind.

The generous monarch granted Juan de Tabares
in fief six towns and villages
of that rugged country. All that he sees
from the high rampart lies under his rule;
no lord in Castile, with power of gallows
and blade, is not in awe of him.

To strengthen him against Moorish pirates,
the king showered him with treasure,
favors, and lands. But yielding to
Lucifer's impious thoughts, cruel and lawless,
he robs, lays waste, burns, and kills—
a more barbarous pirate than those he conquered.

It stuns the eye: his face is calm,
his hair fair, so handsome a face
conceals the instincts of a hyena.
When his rough hunting horn resounds
on the mountain, the mother clutches
her innocent child in silent terror,
and folk flee, afraid of the storm
that threatens them.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Sonnet to My Mother's Doves
translations.text:
To you, doves, I remember you today,
adornments on my house's eaves.
You shape the landscape where I lose myself
to dwell in time that does not pass.

The whitest of you would perch each dusk
upon a pomegranate tree,
and linger like snow upon the green
as evening passed beside her.

You were winged snow and tenderness.
What you are now, pale melting snow,
a faintest memory tries through you
to rescue my other life:

it is the untouched past that keeps alive
the sky of my destroyed childhood.


Sonnet So I Will Not Die

I shall write a sonnet to oppose my death,
a wall built with such strength
that weak and strong will both pass by,
while my name remains as if I lived.

Like a child tumbling down a high stair,
my body will descend into death's embrace.
My body, not my name: my true essence
will be embedded in my sonnet's sturdy wall…

Suddenly I understand: neither now nor later
shall I wrest my name from deserved oblivion.
I cannot save it from the fire's claws,

nor raise it from the dust where it has fallen.
I shall be no more than a muffled plea,
a useless sonnet and a ruined wall.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.text:

translations.title: Grodek
translations.text:
In the evening, deadly weapons resound
in autumn woods; on golden plains
and blue lakes, the sun rolls darker.
Night embraces dying warriors;
their broken mouths burst into wild lament.

But silent on the meadow,
red clouds inhabited by an angry god
summon spilled blood, the chill of the moon;
all roads lead to black decay.

Beneath the golden branches of night and stars,
the sister's shadow wanders through the silent wood,
greeting the heroes' souls,
their bloodied heads.

And in the reed bed sound autumn's dark flutes.
Oh, proud mourning, with bronze altars:
a terrible pain today feeds the spirit's burning flame
for grandchildren yet unborn.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: To the Silenced
translations.text:
In the evening, deadly weapons resound
in autumn woods; on golden plains
and blue lakes, the sun rolls darker.
Night embraces dying warriors;
their broken mouths burst into wild lament.

But silent on the meadow,
red clouds inhabited by an angry god
summon spilled blood, the chill of the moon;
all roads lead to black decay.

Beneath the golden branches of night and stars,
the sister's shadow wanders through the silent wood,
greeting the heroes' souls,
their bloodied heads.

And in the reed bed sound autumn's dark flutes.
Oh, proud mourning, with bronze altars:
a terrible pain today feeds the spirit's burning flame
for grandchildren yet unborn.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Tray
translations.text:
Tray

Nothing more

Lay the head
down on the bedside table

And sleep with the sleep of Holofernes
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Fan
translations.text:
The waltz weeps in my buttonhole

Silence

Sleep has settled on my shoulder
and trembles just like her hair
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Guitar
translations.text:
There will be a green silence,
all made of unraveled guitars.

The guitar is a well
with wind instead of water.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Hawk, Calatañazor...
translations.text:
Hawk, Calatañazor,
toy.
Your gate, a lesser arch,
is so narrow
that no Moor on horseback enters,
and on foot an arrow cannot fit.

Dismount, Almanzor.
Flee quickly.

Down the rugged ravine,
ah, how it tumbled,
toy,
the drum.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: To Manuel Machado
translations.text:
Because his name is Manuel
and Machado his surname,
in his verse Death and Life
play a level game.

Who wins? A draw. And he,
Apollo's banderillero,
knew, sang, and stands alone:
that poet, forged of old,
whose surname is Machado,
and whose name was Manolo.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: Farewell to Pedro Salinas
translations.text:
Silent snail…

Silent snail
in search of the fire
of the obsidian net
where memories fall

from the tiny mirror,
time's scribble,
a taut string of
moonlight

in awakened arpeggios.

Bright and profound shadow,
the margin of your body.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.

translations.title: On horseback in the world's fifth...
translations.text:
(Image)

On horseback in the world's fifth,
a player played yes and no.

Colored rains
migrated to the country of flowers.

Flocks of flowers,
flowers of yes,
flowers of no.

Knives in the air,
that slash his flesh,
form a bridge.

Yes.
No.

The dreamer rides,
harlequin birds

sing yes,
sing no.
translations.editorial_note: Translated directly from the supplied Spanish source; no separate editorial review occurred.
